title: Example Voice Correction: AI-Stink Removal
body:
# Example Voice Correction: AI-Stink Removal

This worked example shows the voice-editor and qa-ai-stink agents in operation. Four passages are shown: the original AI-generated version with annotated problems, and the corrected version with annotation explaining what changed and why. These before/after pairs are the primary training reference for both agents.

---

## Passage 1: Hollow Affirmation Opening

**BEFORE:**
> It is important to note that recommendation systems represent a fundamental shift in how digital products engage with their users. At their core, these systems leverage the power of data to create personalized experiences that resonate with individual preferences.

**AI-STINK PATTERNS DETECTED:**
- "It is important to note" — filler opener that delays the claim
- "represent a fundamental shift" — unearned gravitas; the article has not established why this is fundamental
- "At their core" — hollow stage-setting phrase
- "leverage the power of" — corporate filler
- "resonate with individual preferences" — abstract to the point of meaninglessness

**AFTER:**
> Recommendation systems surface content the user did not know to ask for. That is both the source of their value and the source of their failure modes.

**ANNOTATION:** The corrected version opens with a concrete claim (surfaces content users did not ask for) and immediately connects to the article's argument (value and failure modes). Zero filler words. The reader learns something in the first sentence.

---

## Passage 2: Suspiciously Balanced Conclusion

**BEFORE:**
> Ultimately, whether machine learning recommendations are right for your product depends on a variety of factors. While there are clear advantages to adopting these systems, there are also significant challenges to consider. The best approach is to carefully evaluate your specific situation and make the decision that makes sense for your team and your users.

**AI-STINK PATTERNS DETECTED:**
- "Ultimately" — transition word that signals a non-conclusion is coming
- "Depends on a variety of factors" — refuses to commit to any claim
- "While there are clear advantages... there are also significant challenges" — suspiciously balanced construction that adds no information
- "Carefully evaluate your specific situation" — advice so general it is noise
- "Make the decision that makes sense" — tautology

**AFTER:**
> If your product has fewer than 1,000 monthly active users, do not build a recommendation system yet. You do not have enough interaction data for collaborative filtering to outperform a curated editorial list, and content-based filtering requires item metadata depth most early products do not have. Build the recommendation system when you have the data problem, not before.

**ANNOTATION:** The corrected version takes a position. It gives a specific threshold (1,000 MAU), explains why it is the threshold, and ends with an actionable rule. It is wrong for some edge cases — and that is acceptable. A useful recommendation that is sometimes wrong is more valuable than a correct observation that says nothing.

---

## Passage 3: Oversmooth Transition

**BEFORE:**
> Having explored the different types of recommendation systems available, it is now time to turn our attention to the important question of how these systems can fail. Understanding failure modes is crucial for any team considering implementation.

**AI-STINK PATTERNS DETECTED:**
- "Having explored... it is now time to turn our attention" — artificial chronological narration of the reading experience
- "The important question of" — announces importance rather than demonstrating it
- "Crucial for any team" — hollow intensifier with no specific connection to the reader

**AFTER:**
> Three failure modes cause most recommendation system deployments to underperform. They appear at different stages and require different interventions.

**ANNOTATION:** The corrected transition is two sentences. It tells the reader what the section contains (three failure modes) and why they should read it (they appear at different stages). It does not narrate the act of transitioning — it just transitions.

---

## Passage 4: Imprecise Hedge Stacking

**BEFORE:**
> It is worth noting that it might perhaps be somewhat challenging for smaller teams to implement these more complex approaches, as they may potentially require a level of ML expertise that might not currently be available within the organization.

**AI-STINK PATTERNS DETECTED:**
- "It is worth noting" — filler opener
- "Might perhaps be somewhat" — three hedges stacked on one claim
- "More complex approaches" — vague reference
- "May potentially require" — double hedge
- "Might not currently be" — third layer of uncertainty added unnecessarily

**AFTER:**
> Hybrid recommendation systems require at least one ML engineer with experience in embedding models. Most teams building their first recommendation system do not have this on staff.

**ANNOTATION:** The corrected version is two direct sentences. It names the specific capability gap (ML engineer, embedding models experience) and states the typical hiring reality plainly. The only uncertainty in the original passage was manufactured — the underlying claim is not uncertain at all.
